summary: No. With identical preprocessing applied inside every fold, a default RandomForestClassifier reaches a mean stratified 5-fold CV ROC-AUC of 0.9021 versus 0.9053 for a default LogisticRegression -- the forest is 0.0031 AUC *lower*, winning only 1 of 5 folds. The gap is small enough that the paired 5-fold t-test is not significant (p=0.078), but its sign is consistent: logistic regression came out ahead at all six CV seeds tried (mean difference -0.0039), so the two models are effectively tied with a slight, reproducible edge to logistic regression.
primary_metric_name: Mean stratified 5-fold CV ROC-AUC difference (RF - LogReg)
methodological_choices: Both estimators were left at scikit-learn 1.6.1 defaults as specified (RandomForestClassifier(): 100 trees, unlimited depth; LogisticRegression(): L2, C=1.0, lbfgs, max_iter=100). Preprocessing was held identical for the two models and fit inside each training fold via a Pipeline to avoid leakage: median imputation for the 6 numeric features, most-frequent imputation for the 8 categorical features (workclass/occupation/native-country carry the original '?' missingness, ~2800/2809/857 rows), one-hot encoding with handle_unknown='ignore', and StandardScaler on the numeric block. Scaling is inert for the forest but is what lets default-max_iter lbfgs converge; an unscaled logistic regression does not converge and scores 0.6706 AUC, which would have widened the gap to +0.2315 -- a researcher who skipped scaling would have concluded RF wins by a landslide, purely as an artefact of the optimiser hitting its iteration cap. This is the single choice that most changes the answer. Evaluation: StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42), scoring='roc_auc', with the identical fold split for both models so the per-fold differences are paired (paired t-test on 5 folds). All 48,842 rows retained (duplicates kept, fnlwgt kept as a feature); no class-imbalance handling was applied -- ROC-AUC is threshold-free and the 23.9% positive rate is preserved by stratification, and class_weight='balanced' would change little for a ranking metric. Sensitivity checks: five alternative CV seeds all reproduced the negative sign (range -0.0048 to -0.0034), as did de-duplicating the 52 exact-duplicate rows (-0.0038). Two choices do flip or move it: giving the forest ordinal rather than one-hot categorical encoding lifts it to 0.9058 and nominally ahead (+0.0005, still within seed noise), and dropping fnlwgt costs the forest far more than the regression (0.8912 vs 0.9051), i.e. the unpruned trees are extracting real signal from the census sampling weight that a linear model cannot use. Finally, this compares DEFAULTS, not model classes at their best: the default forest is fully grown with no depth or leaf-size limit, which is its main handicap here, and light tuning (or gradient boosting) would be expected to put tree ensembles clearly ahead.
